lines.text: An illustration: on the first of each month, someone runs a report on the production database — revenue per country, last quarter.
It reads and reads, for many minutes.
Meanwhile, checkout gets slow for every customer.
Same data, same SQL — so why does this one query hurt?
lines.say: Same data, same S Q L — so why does this one query hurt?

lines.text: By the end, you'll know where that report belongs, why its database stores data in columns, and how it answers in seconds.
This is Chapter 3, Part 2, of Martin Kleppmann's book, Designing Data-Intensive Applications.
lines.say: This is Chapter three, Part two, of Martin Klepman's book, Designing Data-Intensive Applications.

lines.text: Part 1 was about storage engines built for looking things up by key — logs, LSM-trees, and B-trees.
lines.say: Part one was about storage engines built for looking things up by key — logs, L S M trees, and B trees.

lines.text: Our monthly report raises three questions. First: why do analytic queries need their own database?
Second: how should that database lay its data out on disk?
And third: can we avoid computing the same answer over and over?
In our story, checkout is online transaction processing, or OLTP; the report is online analytic processing, or OLAP.
lines.say: In our story, checkout is online transaction processing, or O L T P; the report is online analytic processing, or O L A P.

lines.text: Transaction just means a quick group of reads and writes — not necessarily full ACID guarantees.
lines.say: Transaction just means a quick group of reads and writes — not necessarily full acid guarantees.

lines.text: Typically, a transaction reads a few rows by key, while the report aggregates over a huge number of rows.
Transactions write small, random updates as users click; analytics gets its data through bulk imports or streams.
Customers use one side through the app; analysts use the other to make decisions.
One holds the latest state of things; the other holds the history of everything that happened.
And the sizes typically differ: gigabytes to terabytes, versus terabytes to petabytes.
So what happens when both share one database? The report starts a huge scan through the tables.
It competes for the same disks and CPU as every small checkout transaction, so those queue up and slow down.
lines.say: It competes for the same disks and C P U as every small checkout transaction, so those queue up and slow down.

lines.text: That's why the people running these databases are reluctant to let analysts fire ad hoc queries at them.
The usual answer is to give analytics a database of its own.
Part one: data warehousing — a separate database, built for answering questions instead of serving customers. So how does our report's data get there?
In a real company, the data behind our report lives in several OLTP systems: orders, payments, a support tool.
lines.say: In a real company, the data behind our report lives in several O L T P systems: orders, payments, a support tool.

lines.text: First, you extract it, with a periodic dump or a continuous stream of changes.
Then you transform it into a schema that's friendly to analysis, and clean it up along the way.
Finally, you load it into the data warehouse — a separate copy that analysts read but never write to.
That pipeline is called ETL: extract, transform, load.
lines.say: That pipeline is called E T L: extract, transform, load.

lines.text: Now the monthly report can scan as much as it likes, and checkout doesn't feel a thing.
From the outside, a warehouse looks familiar: you still talk to it in SQL, often with the same tools.
lines.say: From the outside, a warehouse looks familiar: you still talk to it in S Q L, often with the same tools.

lines.text: But under the lid, the internals are tuned for a different job — big scans, not lookups by key.
As of the book in 2017, commercial warehouses included Teradata, Vertica, SAP HANA, and ParAccel — Amazon Redshift is a hosted ParAccel.
lines.say: As of the book in twenty seventeen, commercial warehouses included Teradata, Vertica, S A P Hana, and Par Accel — Amazon Redshift is a hosted Par Accel.

lines.text: And there were open-source SQL-on-Hadoop engines, like Apache Hive, Spark SQL, Cloudera Impala, and Facebook's Presto.
lines.say: And there were open-source S Q L on Hadoop engines, like Apache Hive, Spark S Q L, Cloudera Impala, and Facebook's Presto.

lines.text: Inside the warehouse, our report's data usually sits in a star schema, centered on a fact table with one row for every payment.
Some columns describe the payment itself, like amount and fee; others are keys pointing into other tables.
Those are dimension tables: which merchant, who paid, how they paid, where, and when.
Even the date gets its own dimension, so you can record things like public holidays and filter on them.
Draw it out, and the fact table sits in the middle with dimensions around it like rays — hence, a star schema.
Our revenue report is just a sum over the fact table, grouped by region.
Real fact tables are wide: often over a hundred columns, sometimes several hundred.
And they're long: the book describes big enterprises holding tens of petabytes of transaction history, most of it in fact tables.
A variation, the snowflake schema, breaks dimensions into sub-dimensions — a merchant points to its category and its country.
That's more normalized, but stars are often preferred, because they're simpler for analysts to work with.
Keep that width in mind — it's the root of our next problem.
Part two: column storage. Our report touches a few columns of a very wide table — so how should that table sit on disk?
Here's our report as a query: sum the amount, grouped by country, for last quarter's dates.
Out of a hundred-plus columns, it needs just four or five.
But most databases you know, including the engines from Part 1, store data row by row, with all of a row's values together.
lines.say: But most databases you know, including the engines from Part one, store data row by row, with all of a row's values together.

lines.text: So even with an index on the date, the database loads every matching row from disk, every column of it, and parses it.
Then it throws away almost everything it just read, keeping only the few values the report asked for.
Column storage flips this: each column goes into its own file — here, six files for twelve payments, a simplified illustration.
The trick is that every file keeps the same order, so the fourth entry in each file belongs to payment four.
Now a mini version of our report — total amount for Germany: the row store reads all 72 cells, the column store just 24.
lines.say: Now a mini version of our report — total amount for Germany: the row store reads all seventy-two cells, the column store just twenty-four.

lines.text: Now flip the question and fetch every field of payment four: the row store finds it in one place, the column store visits six files.
So it's a trade-off: columns win when you scan many rows but few columns; rows win when you need whole records.
One warning: Cassandra and HBase have column families, but despite the name, they're still mostly row-oriented.
lines.say: One warning: Cassandra and H Base have column families, but despite the name, they're still mostly row-oriented.

lines.text: Columns have another gift: their values repeat. Here's the country column from our twelve payments.
Only three distinct values across twelve rows — and in real life, maybe a few hundred countries across billions of payments.
So for each value, keep a bitmap: one bit per row, set to one wherever that row has the value.
Bitmaps like these are mostly long runs, so store just the run lengths, counting zeros first: Germany becomes 0, 3, 6, 2, 1.
lines.say: Bitmaps like these are mostly long runs, so store just the run lengths, counting zeros first: Germany becomes zero, three, six, two, one.

lines.text: With few distinct values and many rows, the runs get long, and a huge column shrinks to something tiny.
Bitmaps can also answer questions directly. Say the report wants Germany or the Netherlands.
Combine those two bitmaps with a bitwise OR, and you have every matching row.
lines.say: Combine those two bitmaps with a bitwise or, and you have every matching row.

lines.text: Conditions on different columns work too: German payments made by card are the Germany bitmap AND the card bitmap — just payment ten.
lines.say: Conditions on different columns work too: German payments made by card are the Germany bitmap and the card bitmap — just payment ten.

lines.text: That only works because every column file keeps the rows in the same order — the same rule that lined up payment four.
When a warehouse scans millions of rows, a big bottleneck is moving data from disk into memory, and then from memory into the CPU.
lines.say: When a warehouse scans millions of rows, a big bottleneck is moving data from disk into memory, and then from memory into the C P U.

lines.text: Compression helps with both: a chunk of compressed column holds many rows and fits in the CPU's small, fast L1 cache.
lines.say: Compression helps with both: a chunk of compressed column holds many rows and fits in the C P U's small, fast L one cache.

lines.text: The CPU can then run an operation like that bitwise AND straight over the compressed chunk, in a tight loop with no function calls.
lines.say: The C P U can then run an operation like that bitwise and straight over the compressed chunk, in a tight loop with no function calls.

lines.text: The book calls this vectorized processing, and SIMD instructions let one instruction handle many values at once.
lines.say: The book calls this vectorized processing, and sim dee instructions let one instruction handle many values at once.

lines.text: So far, our rows sit in the order they arrived, so the date column jumps around: twelve runs for twelve rows.
You can't just sort one column on its own, though — you'd lose track of which amount belongs to which payment.
Instead, you sort whole rows, even though each column is stored separately — here by date first, then by merchant.
Now a query for June 2 reads only the June 2 block and skips the rest — just what a last-quarter report wants.
lines.say: Now a query for June second reads only the June second block and skips the rest — just what a last-quarter report wants.

lines.text: Sorting helps compression too: the date column drops from twelve runs to three, merchant has eight, and amount stays jumbled.
On billions of rows, the book notes, that first sort column could compress down to a few kilobytes.
Warehouses keep several copies of the data anyway, so that losing a machine doesn't lose data.
C-Store, and later Vertica, had a neat idea: sort each copy differently — by date, by merchant, by country.
lines.say: C Store, and later Vertica, had a neat idea: sort each copy differently — by date, by merchant, by country.

lines.text: Each query then goes to the copy whose order fits it best.
Unlike secondary indexes, which only point to rows stored elsewhere, each sort order holds the actual column values.
All this tidiness has a cost, though: what happens when today's payments arrive?
Squeezing a new row into the middle of sorted, compressed columns would most likely mean rewriting every column file.
The fix comes straight from Part 1's LSM-trees: new writes go into a sorted buffer in memory first.
lines.say: The fix comes straight from Part one's L S M trees: new writes go into a sorted buffer in memory first.

lines.text: When enough have piled up, they're merged with the column files on disk and written out as new files, in bulk.
Queries read both the files and the buffer and combine them, so new data shows up right away — Vertica works this way.
Part three: precomputed aggregates. Our report adds up the same totals every single month — so can we do that work once and reuse it?
Warehouse queries keep asking for the same aggregates — sums, counts, averages, minimums, maximums — over and over.
A regular, virtual view doesn't help: it's just a saved query that gets expanded and rerun every time you read it.
A materialized view actually stores the result on disk, so reading it is cheap.
The catch: whenever the underlying data changes, the view has to be updated too, which makes every write more expensive.
That's why they're rare in OLTP databases, but in a read-heavy warehouse the trade is often worth it.
lines.say: That's why they're rare in O L T P databases, but in a read-heavy warehouse the trade is often worth it.

lines.text: A common special case is the data cube: a grid of totals, here revenue by date and merchant in thousands of dollars — a simplified illustration.
Add up a row and you get one day's total; add up a column and you get one merchant's total — 700 overall.
lines.say: Add up a row and you get one day's total; add up a column and you get one merchant's total — seven hundred overall.

lines.text: Real facts have more dimensions, so the grid grows into a cube, and with five dimensions, a five-dimensional hypercube.
Now Bolt's revenue across all days is a single lookup: 255, already computed.
lines.say: Now Bolt's revenue across all days is a single lookup: two hundred fifty-five, already computed.

lines.text: But ask about payments over 100 dollars, and the cube can't help, because amount isn't one of its dimensions.
lines.say: But ask about payments over one hundred dollars, and the cube can't help, because amount isn't one of its dimensions.

lines.text: So warehouses keep the raw data too, and treat cubes as a speed-up for common queries.
So let's go back to the first of the month, and that report slowing down checkout.
Checkout slowed because analytics and transactions shared one database; ETL into a warehouse separates them.
lines.say: Checkout slowed because analytics and transactions shared one database; E T L into a warehouse separates them.

lines.text: The report read whole rows; a column store reads only the columns it needs, compressed and sorted by date.
And the same totals, recomputed every month, can come from a materialized view or a cube — an answer in seconds, not many minutes.
Now, some questions for your own system. Where do your heavy reports run — on the database serving your users, or on a copy built for analysis?
Which queries scan millions of rows but use only a few columns?
And which totals do you recompute on every dashboard load that could be computed once?
Next is Chapter 4, Encoding and Evolution: how data written by one version of your code gets read by another.
lines.say: Next is Chapter four, Encoding and Evolution: how data written by one version of your code gets read by another.

lines.say: We'll look at formats like Jason, Protocol Buffers, and Avro.
